questions.stem: Economics is the study of how

options.A: scarce resources are used to satisfy unlimited wants
options.B: we choose to use unlimited resources
options.C: limitless resources are used to satisfy scarce wants

explanation_steps: Economics exists because resources are SCARCE (limited) while human wants are UNLIMITED.
The textbook defines economics as the study of how individuals and societies choose to use their scarce resources to satisfy their material wants as much as possible.
B and C reverse the relationship (resources are not unlimited, wants are not scarce); D is wrong because scarcity forces choices. Answer: A.
tips: Remember the pair: scarce RESOURCES – unlimited WANTS. Any option that swaps these words is a distractor.

similar_questions.stem: The basic economic problem that forces every society to make choices is

options.B: scarcity of resources relative to unlimited wants

explanation_steps: Resources are limited while wants are unlimited → scarcity.
Scarcity forces choices about what, how and for whom to produce. Answer: B.

textbook_ref.section: Unit 1 introduction – Scarcity, choice and the definition of economics

questions.stem: A point lies outside the production possibility curve represents:
explanation_steps: Points ON the PPC use all resources fully → efficient.
Points INSIDE the PPC are attainable but inefficient (unused or badly used resources).
Points OUTSIDE (beyond) the PPC cannot be produced with the currently available resources and technology → unattainable. Answer: C.
tips: Inside = inefficient, On = efficient, Outside = unattainable (until resources or technology increase and the PPC shifts outward).

similar_questions.stem: On a production possibilities curve, a point lying inside the curve shows that

options.A: the economy is producing at full efficiency
options.B: some resources are unemployed or used inefficiently

explanation_steps: Inside the curve the economy could produce more of both goods.
So resources are idle or used inefficiently. Answer: B.

textbook_ref.section: 1.1.3 Production Possibilities Curve (PPC)

questions.stem: _____ refers to those man-made physical goods used to produce other goods or services.
explanation_steps: The four factors of production are land, labour, capital and entrepreneurship.
Capital = man-made physical goods used to produce other goods and services (machines, tools, buildings, roads). Its reward is interest.
Land is natural (not man-made); labour is human effort; entrepreneurship is decision making and risk taking. Answer: B.
tips: 'Man-made + used to produce other goods' is the textbook signal for CAPITAL.

similar_questions.stem: The reward (payment) for the factor of production 'capital' is called
explanation_steps: Land → rent; labour → wage/salary; capital → interest; entrepreneurship → profit.
Answer: C.

textbook_ref.section: 1.1.1 Types of Factors of Production

questions.stem: All of the following are characteristics of free market economy except:
explanation_steps: Figure 1.3 of the Grade 10 textbook ('Characteristics of Free Enterprise and Capitalism') lists: economic freedom, voluntary exchange, private property rights, profit motive and competition.
Options A–D are ALL characteristics of a free market (capitalist) economy, so none of them is the exception.
Answer: E (None of the above).
tips: In 'except' questions, check every option; when all of A–D are true, the answer is 'None of the above'.

similar_questions.stem: Which of the following is a characteristic of a command (centrally planned) economy?

options.B: Prices determined by supply and demand
options.C: Major economic decisions made by a central planning authority

explanation_steps: In a command economy resources are publicly owned and a central planning authority (the government) decides what, how and for whom to produce.
A, B, D and E describe a free market economy. Answer: C.

textbook_ref.section: Unit 1 introduction – (ii) Economic Systems: capitalist/free market system
textbook_ref.note: The list of characteristics is in Figure 1.3 (image on printed p.6); checked visually on the PDF page.

questions.stem: A firm that takes the form of an independent legal entity with ownership divide in to shares is
explanation_steps: The textbook: 'A corporation is a firm that takes the form of an independent legal entity with ownership divided into shares.'
A sole trader and a partnership are not separate legal entities (owners have unlimited liability); a cooperative is formed to serve its members. Answer: B.
tips: Shares + separate legal entity + limited liability = corporation.

similar_questions.stem: The profit of a corporation that is distributed to its shareholders is called
explanation_steps: Shareholders are the owners of a corporation.
The part of profit paid to them is a dividend. Answer: B.

textbook_ref.section: 1.2 Business Organizations – C. Corporation

questions.stem: One of the following is not the advantage of corporation?
explanation_steps: Advantages of a corporation in the textbook: (i) limited liability, (ii) continuity, (iii) large size business (it can raise large capital by selling shares), (iv) easy to employ professional employees.
All of A–D are advantages, so none is the exception. Answer: E.
Disadvantages (for contrast): double taxation, large initial cost, possible conflict between management and owners.
tips: Learn the advantage/disadvantage lists of each business form – they are frequently tested as 'except' questions.

similar_questions.stem: Which of the following is a DISADVANTAGE of a corporation?
explanation_steps: Corporate profit is taxed, and dividends are taxed again as shareholders' income → double taxation.
The other options are advantages. Answer: C.

textbook_ref.section: 1.2 Business Organizations – Advantages of corporation

explanation_steps: The textbook lists four modern communication systems: visual, acoustic, telecommunication and data-processing.
'Telephone, telegraph and record player are examples of acoustic systems.'
Television is treated as a visual/telecommunication system. So telephone (A) and telegraph (C) → Answer: E.

similar_questions.stem: Holography, copying machines and video systems are examples of which type of communication system?
explanation_steps: The textbook classifies holography, copying machines and video as visual systems.

questions.stem: A type of metallic money in which the value of the metallic content of the coin is equal to its face value is called
explanation_steps: Metallic money is divided into standard coins and token coins.
'Standard coins are also known as full bodied coins. If the value of the metallic content of the coin is equal to the face value, the coin is known as full bodied coin.'
Token coins have a face value greater than the metal value. So both A and C name the same coin → Answer: E.
tips: Standard coin = full-bodied coin (metal value = face value); token coin: face value > metal value.

similar_questions.stem: Most coins in use today, whose face value is greater than the value of the metal they contain, are called

questions.stem: Mr. Merih borrows money to buy a house from commercial bank of Eritrea, his future commitment will be agreed to pay his debt in Nakfa. In this case money functions as
explanation_steps: Money has four functions: medium of exchange, unit of account, store of value, standard of deferred payments.
Borrowing now and agreeing to repay LATER in Nakfa uses money as the standard for future (deferred) payments – the textbook uses this exact house-loan example.
Answer: C.
tips: Deferred = postponed. Loans, credit and debts → standard of deferred payment.

similar_questions.stem: When prices of all goods in a shop are expressed in Nakfa so that they can be compared, money is working as a
explanation_steps: Measuring and comparing values in a common unit is the unit-of-account function.
Answer: B.

questions.stem: All of the following are functions of central/national bank except

options.B: Acts as banker, agent and financial adviser to the government

explanation_steps: The textbook lists the essential functions of a central (national) bank: (a) issue bank notes/currency, (b) banker, agent and financial adviser to the government, (c) hold member banks' cash reserves, (d) lender of last resort.
Accepting deposits from the public and granting loans are functions of COMMERCIAL banks; a central bank does not deal directly with the public.
Answer: E.
tips: Central bank = bank of the government and bankers' bank. Commercial bank = bank of the public (deposits and loans).

similar_questions.stem: Which of the following is a function of a commercial bank rather than of the central bank?

options.B: Keeping the cash reserves of other banks
options.C: Lending to individuals and small businesses
options.D: Acting as lender of last resort

explanation_steps: A commercial bank mobilises deposits and lends to the public.
The other options are central-bank functions. Answer: C.

textbook_ref.section: 2.2.1 Types of Banks – Functions of a Central Bank (National Bank)

questions.stem: Which of the following bank give loans to poor households and small business sector?
explanation_steps: The textbook: the Savings and Micro-Credit Program (SMCP) extends financial resources to poor households and small business enterprises that could not get loans from formal banks.
Answer: D.
tips: Eritrean financial institutions in the textbook: Bank of Eritrea (central), Commercial Bank of Eritrea, Housing and Commerce Bank, Eritrean Development and Investment Bank and the Savings and Micro-Credit Program.

similar_questions.stem: Which Eritrean financial institution provides loans for investment but does NOT mobilise savings of the public?
explanation_steps: The textbook states the Eritrean Development and Investment Bank does not mobilise public savings; it provides investment loans.
Answer: B.

textbook_ref.section: 2.2.2 Banks in Eritrea – Savings and Micro-Credit Program (SMCP)

questions.stem: The possibility of loss or no loss is transferred from the insured to the insurer. This insurance characteristic implies
explanation_steps: Basic characteristics of insurance: sharing of losses, payment of accidental losses, risk transfer and indemnification.
Textbook: 'Risk transfer means that the possibility of loss or no loss is transferred from the insured to the insurer.'
Answer: C. (Insurable interest is a legal principle, not a characteristic.)
tips: Characteristics (4): pooling/sharing, accidental losses, risk transfer, indemnification. Legal principles (5): indemnity, insurable interest, subrogation, utmost good faith, contribution.

similar_questions.stem: Restoring the insured to approximately the same financial position as before the loss is called
explanation_steps: This is the textbook definition of indemnification.
Answer: C.

textbook_ref.section: 2.3.1 Basic Characteristics of Insurance – c. Risk Transfer

questions.stem: Which principle of insurance states that an individual should not claim compensation from two sources?
explanation_steps: The Grade 10 textbook states word for word: 'The principle of subrogation is that an individual should not claim compensation from two sources.'
Example in the book: Saba's insured car is damaged by Haile. After the insurer pays Saba, she cannot also claim from Haile; the insurer takes over (is subrogated to) her right to claim from Haile.
Contribution applies when the same property is insured with more than one insurer (insurers share the loss); indemnity says the insured must not profit from a loss.
Answer: B (textbook definition).
tips: Trap: 'two sources' sounds like contribution, but the textbook sentence belongs to SUBROGATION (insurer + guilty third party = the two sources).

similar_questions.stem: After paying a claim to its client, an insurance company takes over the client's right to recover the loss from the careless person who caused it. This is the principle of
explanation_steps: The insurer steps into the shoes of the insured to claim from the guilty party → subrogation.
Answer: C.

textbook_ref.section: 2.3.2 Legal Principles of Insurance – iii. Principle of subrogation

questions.review_flag: Many general texts would associate 'not receiving compensation twice' with indemnity/contribution; the key B follows the textbook's exact wording.

questions.stem: A monopolist will

options.A: fixes the price and level of output of his/her product simultaneously
options.B: always sells a product which is a necessity for the buyers or consumers
options.D: be able to increase its market size by increasing its product

explanation_steps: Textbook (G11 p.5): 'A monopolist has the power to EITHER fix the price at which he/she wants to sell OR the quantity he/she wishes to sell' – not both at once, because it faces the market demand curve. So A is false.
B is false: a monopoly product need not be a necessity. C is false: a monopolist faces a DOWNWARD-sloping demand curve (a horizontal demand curve belongs to a firm in perfect competition).

D is the only option that can be defended: because the monopolist is the whole industry and faces the downward-sloping market demand curve, it can sell more (enlarge the quantity sold in its market) by producing more and lowering the price.
E is false because A–C are false. Best available answer: D (low confidence – see review flag).
tips: Monopoly facts to remember: single seller, no close substitutes, high entry barriers, price maker, downward-sloping demand, can fix price OR output but not both.

similar_questions.stem: Which of the following is TRUE of a monopolist?

options.A: It faces a horizontal demand curve
options.B: It can fix either the price or the quantity sold, but not both
options.C: It sells a homogeneous product in competition with many firms
options.D: There are no barriers to entry

explanation_steps: The monopolist faces the downward-sloping market demand curve: once it chooses a price, buyers decide the quantity (or vice versa).
A, C, D and E describe perfect competition. Answer: B.

textbook_ref.section: 1.1.1 Market Structure – a) Monopoly

questions.review_flag: No option is clearly correct. A contradicts the textbook ('either price or quantity', not both); B, C and E are false. D ('increase its market size by increasing its product') is awkwardly worded and only defensible loosely. Keyed D as the least-wrong option; the setter may have intended A (misreading the textbook). Needs teacher decision.

questions.stem: A market where there are few consumers for goods and services is;
explanation_steps: Buyer-side imperfect markets: monopsony = only ONE buyer; oligopsony = a FEW buyers.
Seller side: monopoly = one seller; oligopoly = few sellers.
Few consumers (buyers) → oligopsony. Answer: D.
tips: '-poly' = sellers, '-psony' = buyers; 'mono' = one, 'oligo' = few.

similar_questions.stem: A town where the government is the only employer of teachers is an example of
explanation_steps: There is only one buyer of teachers' labour.
Single buyer → monopsony. Answer: B.

textbook_ref.section: 1.1.1 Market Structure – Monopsony and Oligopsony

questions.stem: Which of the following is not a characteristic of a perfect competition market?

options.A: large number of buyers and sellers
options.D: perfect mobility of labour and capital
options.E: freedom of entry and exit to and from the market

explanation_steps: Characteristics of perfect competition: many buyers and sellers, HOMOGENEOUS (identical) products, perfect information, perfect mobility, freedom of entry and exit.
Differentiated products belong to monopolistic competition (and differentiated oligopoly). Answer: B.
tips: Homogeneous = identical products; differentiated = brand names, designs, packaging.

similar_questions.stem: Many sellers selling similar but differentiated products (e.g. restaurants, car repair shops) is called
explanation_steps: Many sellers + differentiated products + few entry barriers = monopolistic competition.
Answer: C.

textbook_ref.section: 1.1.1 Market Structure – i) Perfect competition

questions.stem: Demand for Veblen goods actually rises when
explanation_steps: Veblen goods (goods of ostentation) are bought to show status; some consumers believe a higher price means better quality.
So for these goods quantity demanded rises when the price rises – an exception to the law of demand. Answer: A.
tips: Exceptions to the law of demand in the textbook: Giffen goods and Veblen goods (e.g. jewellery, certain car brands).

similar_questions.stem: Which of the following is an exception to the law of demand?
explanation_steps: For Giffen goods (very cheap staples) a price rise can increase quantity demanded.
Answer: C.

textbook_ref.section: 1.2 Demand and Supply – Exceptions to the law of demand: b) Veblen goods

questions.stem: Which of the following pairs of goods represents complementary products?
explanation_steps: Complementary goods are goods that are jointly consumed/used (textbook example: car and gasoline).
Computer and software, brick and cement, car and petroleum are all used together → complements.
Butter and margarine can replace each other → substitutes. Answer: E (all except A).
tips: Test: if the price of one rises and demand for the other FALLS → complements; if demand for the other RISES → substitutes.

similar_questions.stem: Tea and coffee are usually considered
explanation_steps: Either can be used in place of the other.
Answer: B.

textbook_ref.section: 1.2 Demand and Supply – Price of related goods and services

questions.stem: If an increase in the income results in a decrease in the quantity demanded of a good, then the good is;
explanation_steps: Textbook: 'In the case of inferior goods, an increase in income will lead to a decrease in the quantity of that good demanded. The income elasticity of an inferior good is negative.'
Answer: C.
tips: Income elasticity: inferior < 0; necessity between 0 and 1; luxury > 1.

similar_questions.stem: If a 20% rise in income causes a 10% FALL in the quantity demanded of second-hand clothes, the income elasticity of demand is
explanation_steps: Income elasticity = %ΔQ ÷ %ΔY = −10% ÷ 20% = −0.5.
Negative → inferior good. Answer: C.

textbook_ref.section: 1.3.1 Elasticity of Demand – c) Income elasticity of demand

questions.stem: If a 10 per cent decrease in the price of a good result in a 30% increase in the quantity demanded, the price elasticity of demand for the good will be_____.
explanation_steps: Ped = % change in quantity demanded ÷ % change in price = 30% ÷ (−10%) = −3.
The minus sign is conventionally dropped → Ped = 3 (elastic). Answer: A.
tips: Always put %ΔQ on top: 'Quantity over Price'.

similar_questions.stem: If a 20% increase in the price of sugar reduces quantity demanded by 5%, the price elasticity of demand is
explanation_steps: Ped = 5% ÷ 20% = 0.25 (ignoring the minus sign).
Less than 1 → inelastic. Answer: B.

textbook_ref.section: 1.3.1 Elasticity of Demand – a) Price elasticity of demand

questions.stem: If price elasticity of demand is greater than one, demand is said to be _____.
explanation_steps: Ped > 1 → elastic; Ped = 1 → unitary elastic; Ped < 1 → inelastic; Ped = 0 → perfectly inelastic; Ped = ∞ → perfectly elastic.
Answer: C.
tips: Elastic demand: a price cut RAISES total expenditure (total expenditure test).

similar_questions.stem: If a fall in the price of a good leaves consumers' total expenditure on it unchanged, demand is
explanation_steps: Total expenditure test: no change in expenditure when price changes → Ped = 1.
Answer: C.

textbook_ref.section: 1.3.1 Elasticity of Demand – Types of price elasticity; total expenditure test

questions.stem: If the output of a firm is zero in the short run then:

options.B: it will have only fixed costs
options.D: it will have very large variable costs

explanation_steps: In the short run some inputs (buildings, machinery, rent, insurance) are fixed; their costs must be paid even if nothing is produced.
Variable costs are zero when output is zero. So TC = TFC at Q = 0. Answer: B.
tips: TC = TFC + TVC. At zero output TVC = 0, so TC = TFC.

similar_questions.stem: Which of the following is a fixed cost for a bakery in the short run?
explanation_steps: Rent does not change with the number of loaves produced.
Answer: C.

textbook_ref.section: 1.4 Cost of Production – short-term fixed and variable costs

questions.stem: The short run cost function of X-company is given by the following equation TC = 1,900 + 53Q where TC is Total Cost and Q is the quantity of output produced. If the company produces 100 units what will be its TVC?
explanation_steps: In TC = 1,900 + 53Q, the constant 1,900 is total fixed cost (it does not change with Q) and 53Q is total variable cost.
tips: Constant term = TFC; the term containing Q = TVC; 53 is the variable cost per unit (AVC = MC = 53).

similar_questions.stem: A firm's total cost is TC = 2,500 + 40Q. What is its total variable cost when Q = 50?
explanation_steps: Answer: A.

textbook_ref.section: 1.4 Cost of Production – TC = TFC + TVC

questions.stem: The short run cost function of X-company is given by the following equation TC = 1,900 + 53Q where TC is Total Cost and Q is the quantity of output produced. What is the total cost of producing 100 units?
tips: Check: TC − TFC must equal TVC (7,200 − 1,900 = 5,300).

similar_questions.stem: For TC = 2,500 + 40Q, what is the total cost of producing 50 units?
explanation_steps: Answer: B.

textbook_ref.section: 1.4 Cost of Production – TC = TFC + TVC

questions.stem: The income of individuals after payment of personal taxes is:
explanation_steps: Disposable Personal Income (Yd) = Personal Income − personal taxes: the income households actually have to spend or save.
Answer: D.
tips: Chain: GNP → (−depreciation) NNP → (−indirect business taxes) NI → PI → (−personal taxes) Yd → (−consumption) personal saving.

similar_questions.stem: If personal income is Nakfa 8,000 and personal taxes are Nakfa 1,200, disposable personal income is
explanation_steps: Yd = PI − personal taxes = 8,000 − 1,200 = 6,800.
Answer: B.

explanation_steps: Expenditure approach: GDP = C + I + G + (X − M).
Textbook: 'Personal consumption expenditure (C) is the largest component of the aggregate expenditure.' Answer: C.
tips: Remember C + I + G + NX; C (household spending) is always the biggest share.

similar_questions.stem: Using the expenditure approach, GDP equals
explanation_steps: The expenditure approach adds spending on final goods: consumption, investment, government purchases and net exports.
Answer: A.

questions.stem: Per capita income is

options.A: Gross domestic product divided by national income
options.B: Gross national product multiplied by disposable income
options.C: Net national product divided by population
options.D: Gross domestic product divided by population
options.E: Gross national product divided by employed population

explanation_steps: Textbook: 'Per capita income is a country's GDP or GNP divided by its population.'
Option D (GDP ÷ population) matches exactly. C uses NNP, E divides by EMPLOYED population only, A and B are meaningless. Answer: D.
tips: Per capita = per head of the WHOLE population (not only the employed).

similar_questions.stem: A country has a GDP of Nakfa 900 million and a population of 3 million. Its per capita income is
explanation_steps: Per capita income = 900,000,000 ÷ 3,000,000 = Nakfa 300.
Answer: B.

questions.stem: If the price of wheat declines, a consumer will buy

options.A: fewer wheat, so that their marginal utility will increase
options.B: fewer wheat, so that marginal utility will decrease
options.C: more wheat, so that their marginal utility will increase
options.D: more wheat, so that their marginal utility will decrease

explanation_steps: The consumer is in equilibrium when MU/P is the same for every good (MUA/PA = MUB/PB).
A fall in the price of wheat raises MU/P for wheat, so the consumer buys MORE wheat.

By the law of diminishing marginal utility, consuming more wheat LOWERS its marginal utility until MU/P is equal again (textbook example: bread price falls from Nakfa 2 to 1, Haile buys 4 instead of 2 and MU falls from 20 to 10). Answer: D.
tips: Lower price → buy more → MU falls. This is how the downward-sloping demand curve is derived.

similar_questions.stem: A consumer is in equilibrium buying bread (MU = 20, price Nakfa 2) and milk (MU = 30, price Nakfa 3). If the price of milk rises, she will

options.A: buy more milk so its MU falls
options.B: buy less milk so its MU rises
options.C: buy the same amount of milk
options.E: buy more milk so its MU rises

explanation_steps: A higher price lowers MU/P for milk below MU/P for bread.
She buys less milk; with fewer units, milk's MU rises until MU/P are equal again. Answer: B.

textbook_ref.section: 1.5 Consumer Choice and Demand – consumer equilibrium and deriving the demand curve

questions.stem: Which of the following are not properties of indifference curve?

options.C: indifference curve bowed inward the origin
options.D: indifference curve cannot cross each other

explanation_steps: Properties in the textbook: (1) negative (downward) slope, (2) bowed inward toward the origin (convex), (3) curves further to the north-east show higher satisfaction, (4) indifference curves cannot intersect.
A positive slope is NOT a property. Answer: A.
tips: Negative slope because to keep satisfaction constant, more of one good must mean less of the other.

similar_questions.stem: An indifference curve is convex (bowed inward toward the origin) because of
explanation_steps: As the consumer gets more food, he is willing to give up less and less clothing for one more unit of food.
This diminishing MRS makes the curve flatter → convex. Answer: B.

textbook_ref.section: 1.5 Consumer Choice and Demand – Properties of indifference curves

explanation_steps: Answer: B.

explanation_steps: Answer: B.

options.A: how the government raises revenue only
options.B: how the government raises revenue and makes expenditure only

questions.stem:
What are the four types of factors of production? (4 points)
a. _____   b. _____   c. _____   d. _____
questions.answer: a. Land   b. Labour   c. Capital   d. Entrepreneurship
explanation_steps: Factors of production are the resources used to produce goods and services.
Land – all naturally occurring resources (soil, minerals, water, forests); fixed in quantity; reward = rent.
Labour – human physical and mental effort used in production; reward = wage/salary.
Capital – man-made physical goods used to produce other goods (machines, tools, buildings, roads); reward = interest.
Entrepreneurship – decision making and risk taking to organise the other factors; reward = profit.
tips: Learn them with their rewards: Land–rent, Labour–wage, Capital–interest, Entrepreneurship–profit.
'Money' is NOT a factor of production in the textbook; physical capital is.

similar_questions.stem: Name the reward (factor income) earned by each factor of production: land, labour, capital and entrepreneurship.
similar_questions.answer: Land → rent; Labour → wages/salaries; Capital → interest; Entrepreneurship → profit.
explanation_steps: Each factor owner is paid for the service of the factor.
These four incomes added together make up national income (income approach).

questions.stem: Define the following: A) national income (1 point)  B) exchange rate (1 point)  C) barter system (1 point)
questions.answer:
A) National income is the sum of all incomes earned by the factors of production owned by a country's citizens in a period of one year, i.e. the total of wages, rent, interest and profit (in the textbook's chain of measures NI = NNP minus indirect business taxes, plus subsidies).
B) The exchange rate is the rate at which one currency is exchanged for another currency, i.e. the price of one currency in terms of another (e.g. 1 USD = Nakfa 15).
C) A barter system is the exchange of goods for goods (or services) without the use of money.

subparts.label: A
subparts.question: National income
subparts.answer: The sum of all incomes (wages, rent, interest and profit) earned by the factors of production owned by a country's citizens in one year.
steps: Key words: incomes of factors of production; citizens of the country; one year.

subparts.label: B
subparts.question: Exchange rate
subparts.answer: The rate at which one currency is exchanged for another; the price of one currency in terms of another (e.g. 1 USD = Nakfa 15).
steps: Key words: rate/price; one currency in terms of another.

subparts.label: C
subparts.question: Barter system
subparts.answer: The exchange of goods for goods (and services) without the use of money.

National income measures the total factor income of a country's citizens in a year.
Exchange rate is a ratio/price between two currencies (determined in the foreign exchange market).
Barter is direct exchange without money; its main difficulty is the lack of a double coincidence of wants.

questions.stem:
Price of wheat per quintal (in Nakfa) / Quantity of wheat demanded (in quintals): 300 / 30; 200 / 35; 100 / 50.
What is the price elasticity of demand of wheat when its price increases from Nakfa 200 to Nakfa 300 per quintal? (3 points)
questions.answer:
Ped = [(30 − 35)/35] ÷ [(300 − 200)/200] = (−14.29%) ÷ (50%) = −0.2857 ≈ −0.29. Ignoring the sign, Ped ≈ 0.29 (0.28 if %ΔQ is first rounded to −14%, as in the textbook). Since Ped < 1, the demand for wheat is inelastic: a 10% rise in price reduces quantity demanded by about 2.9%.

Calculation (textbook formula: changes measured from the ORIGINAL values P₁ = 200, Q₁ = 35)
Step                          | Working                                    |               Result
------------------------------+--------------------------------------------+---------------------
% change in quantity demanded | (Q₂ − Q₁)/Q₁ × 100 = (30 − 35)/35 × 100    |              −14.29%
% change in price             | (P₂ − P₁)/P₁ × 100 = (300 − 200)/200 × 100 |                 +50%
Price elasticity of demand    | Ped = −14.29% ÷ 50%                        | −0.29 → |Ped| ≈ 0.29
Interpretation                | 0.29 < 1                                   |     Inelastic demand

answer_tables.title: Calculation (textbook formula: changes measured from the ORIGINAL values P₁ = 200, Q₁ = 35)

explanation_steps: Identify the original and new values: P₁ = 200, P₂ = 300; Q₁ = 35, Q₂ = 30 (a price INCREASE from 200 to 300).
% change in quantity demanded = (30 − 35)/35 × 100 = −14.29%.
The minus sign is conventionally dropped: Ped ≈ 0.29 (< 1) → inelastic demand.
This is the textbook's Table 1.7 example with all values divided by 10 (textbook answer: −14/50 = −0.28).
marking_points: Correct formula Ped = %ΔQd ÷ %ΔP using original values (1)
tips: Use the ORIGINAL price and quantity (before the change) as the base – that is the formula in the Grade 11 textbook.
Accept 0.28–0.29 (rounding). Do not use the midpoint formula unless the question asks for it (it would give ≈ 0.38).
Total expenditure check: 200 × 35 = 7,000 → 300 × 30 = 9,000; spending rises when price rises → inelastic, consistent with Ped < 1.
